title: Damping, forced oscillations and resonance; Gas laws and ideal gas equation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: O04-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; O04-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; O04-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; O04-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: O04-1#N.2a, O04-uk1#N.3, T05-1#N.2a, O04-1#N.4a, O04-uk1#N.5, T05-1#N.6, O04-1#N.10a, O04-uk1#N.10, T05-1#N.9a, T05-1#N.12.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Forced oscillation
items.clue: Motion kept going by a periodic driver, which sets its steady rate.

items.label: Natural frequency
items.clue: Symbol f₀: cycles per second of a system that is displaced, let go and left alone.

items.label: Free oscillation
items.clue: Motion after a system is displaced and released, with nothing further acting on it.

items.label: Light damping
items.clue: Condition in which the amplitude falls by roughly the same fraction on every cycle.

questions.stem: A lightly damped mass–spring system has a natural frequency of 2.0 Hz. It is driven by a periodic force of constant amplitude with a frequency of 3.5 Hz. Which describes its oscillation once the amplitude has become steady?

options.text: At 3.5 Hz, with a smaller amplitude than when driven at 2.0 Hz
At 2.0 Hz, its natural frequency, with a small steady amplitude
At 3.5 Hz, with a larger amplitude than when it is driven at 2.0 Hz
At 3.5 Hz, with the same amplitude as when it is driven at 2.0 Hz

questions.stem: A lightly damped mass–spring system is released with an amplitude of 60 mm. After one complete oscillation its amplitude is 45 mm. The amplitude falls by the same fraction in each oscillation. What is the amplitude after three complete oscillations?

options.text: 15 mm
25 mm
34 mm
30 mm

questions.explanation: Each amplitude is 0.75 × the previous one: 60 × 0.75³ = 25 mm.

questions.stem: A cylinder contains 0.64 kg of oxygen gas, which consists of O₂ molecules. The molar mass of oxygen atoms is 16 g mol⁻¹, and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many oxygen molecules are in the cylinder?
In its spin cycle, a washing machine's drum speeds up steadily. At one rotation rate the whole machine shakes violently; at higher rates it runs smoothly again. Why does it shake at that one rate?

options.text: It is then rotating fastest, so it transfers the most energy per second.
The rotation rate then equals a natural frequency of the machine.
The damping in the machine's mounts falls to zero at that rotation rate.
It is no longer forced: the machine now oscillates freely at its own frequency.

questions.explanation: The spinning drum drives the machine. When the driving frequency matches a natural frequency, energy builds up each cycle: resonance, maximum amplitude.

questions.stem: Damping reduces the amplitude of a mass–spring oscillator from 40 mm to 20 mm. What fraction of the original oscillation energy has been transferred to the surroundings?

options.text: None, because the period has not changed

questions.explanation: E ∝ A². Half the amplitude leaves 1/4 of the energy, so 3/4 has been transferred to the surroundings.

questions.stem: Predict first. Students measure the pressure of three samples of gas, each sealed in a rigid container, at several temperatures between 0 °C and 100 °C. The samples are of different gases and different amounts, and each behaves as an ideal gas. For each sample they plot pressure against temperature in °C and get a straight line. They then extend each best-fit line to zero pressure. What do they find?

options.text: All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, 0 °C.
All three lines reach zero pressure at the same temperature, about −273 °C.
The steepest line reaches zero pressure at the highest temperature.
Each line reaches zero pressure at a temperature set by its kind of gas.

questions.stem: A singer shatters a wine glass by singing one steady note close to it. Which condition is essential for this to happen?

options.text: The note is very loud, whatever frequency the singer chooses.
The note is the highest frequency that the singer is able to produce.
The note's frequency is equal to a natural frequency of the glass.
The sound echoes inside the bowl of the glass and builds up.

questions.stem: A car's wing mirror buzzes violently at one engine speed. A rubber damper is fitted to the mirror's mounting. What happens now as the engine passes that speed?

options.text: The violent buzzing moves to a much higher engine speed.
The mirror stops responding to the engine at all.
It still buzzes most near the same engine speed, but far less.
It now buzzes strongly at every engine speed.

questions.explanation: Damping removes energy every cycle. The resonance peak stays at about the same frequency but is much lower (and broader).

questions.stem: A bubble of gas of volume 2.0 cm³ is released at the bottom of a lake, where the pressure is 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the temperature is 7 °C. It rises to the surface, where the pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the temperature is 17 °C. Treat the gas as ideal, with no gas gained or lost. What is its volume at the surface?

options.text: 6.0 cm³
15 cm³
6.2 cm³
0.69 cm³

questions.explanation: pressure × volume ÷ T is constant: V₂ = 2.0 × (3.0 × 10⁵/1.0 × 10⁵) × (290/280) = 6.2 cm³.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container holds an ideal gas at 7 °C. The gas is heated to 287 °C. How does its new pressure compare with its starting pressure?

options.text: It is the same, because the container is rigid, so the volume cannot change.
It is 41 times as large, because the temperature has risen from 7 °C to 287 °C.
It is twice as large, because the absolute temperature doubles, from 280 K to 560 K.
It is 1.4 times as large, because the molecules move √2 times as fast.

questions.explanation: At constant volume, pressure ÷ absolute temperature is constant. 560 K/280 K = 2.
